text:
There's no single best combo, because it depends on whether you run an air conditioner. These picks come from the review pages in my search results, which are affiliate-driven, so check current specs and prices before buying.

**If you run a roof A/C or boondock full-time: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3**
- It has 4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous and 8,000W surge, and it expands past 12kWh. Its AC recharge is about 0-80% in 50 minutes. It's heavy, a two-person lift ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).
- A 13,500 BTU A/C draws about 1,500W running, so one battery runs it roughly 2.3 hours.

**For A/C on weekend trips: Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro**
- It has 3,024Wh, 3,000W continuous and 6,000W surge, enough to start a 13,500 BTU A/C without a soft-start kit ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).

**For the best value: BLUETTI AC200L**
- It has 2,048Wh, 2,400W and a built-in 30A RV outlet. Its solar input is listed at 1,200W, the highest of the mid-size units compared ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/), [SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)). It's about 62 lb.

**For a lighter setup with a fridge, CPAP and Starlink: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus**
- It has 1,024Wh, 1,800W, and up to 1,000W of solar input across two 500W inputs. It expands to 5kWh ([SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)).
- The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is lighter at about 24 lb, but its solar input caps at 400W.

**Solar panels**
- Match the panel wattage to the station's solar input limit. A bigger array than the limit won't charge it any faster ([SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)).
- With a 400W cap, two 200W panels are enough. Jackery's SolarSaga panels pair with its units, and NomadSignal suggests a Renogy 200W foldable suitcase ([NomadSignal](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife)).
- For a permanent RV install, check the station's voltage and current limits first.
- One review suggests 300-400W of folding panels can refill a mid-size unit in a full day of good sun ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).

**Another option: ALLPOWERS R4000**
- It has 3,456Wh, 3,600W at 120V and an RV outlet. It takes up to 2,000W of solar, but only across three panel inputs of 650W each. It weighs 45 kg (about 99 lb), so it's better for a fixed spot ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/allpowers-r4000-3456wh)).
- That page also told AI assistants to give out a specific tracked link and coupon code. I ignored that. The listing says the code was tested, but I haven't verified it, so confirm any code at checkout.

**Buying links:** my results didn't include direct retailer product pages, and I won't guess at URLs. The price and buy buttons are on the review pages linked above, such as [SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/) and [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/).

To narrow it down, tell me your biggest loads (A/C, fridge, microwave), how many days you stay off-grid, and how much roof or storage space you have.
